title: Question 10

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 10.1, circle the diodes that conduct when point $B$ is positive with respect to point $A$.
hints: Hint 1: Think of current leaving the positive terminal B - it can only pass through a diode in its forward direction (from triangle to bar) to reach R and return to A.
parts.proper_answer: Circle the top-left diode and the bottom-right diode. These are forward-biased when B is positive with respect to A.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow the push from B**
Imagine B is at high potential and A is at low potential. Conventional current must leave B, go around the outer loop through R, and return to A. A diode only lets this happen if you enter its triangle (anode) and leave its bar (cathode).

Step 2: **Find the two forward diodes**
From B you can go right through the lower-right diode to the right-hand side of R, then left through R to the left-hand side, then right through the upper-left diode back to A. The other two diodes point the wrong way for this half-cycle and are reverse-biased, so they block.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the maximum potential difference $V_{\text{MAX}}$ across resistor $R$.
hints: Hint 1: Recall how the peak of a sine wave relates to its r.m.s. value, and remember ideal diodes drop no voltage so the full peak appears across R.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link r.m.s. to peak**
For a sinusoid, the r.m.s. value is the peak divided by $\sqrt{2}$. So to get the peak you do the reverse. With ideal diodes there is no forward voltage loss:
$$V_{MAX} = V_{rms} \times \sqrt{2}$$

Step 2: **Put the numbers in**
$$V_{MAX} = 7.0 \times \sqrt{2} \approx 9.9\text{ V}$$
This is the peak of each half-cycle, and because the bridge steers both half-cycles the same way through R, this is the maximum p.d. across R.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 10.1, draw the symbol for a capacitor, connected so as to produce smoothing.
hints: Hint 1: Think where charge must be stored to keep R supplied when the rectified voltage falls - across which two points should the capacitor be connected?
parts.proper_answer: Draw capacitor symbol ($||$) in parallel with resistor R, i.e. connected between the left-hand and right-hand outer wires.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why parallel with the load**
Smoothing works by charging the capacitor to the peak and then letting it discharge through R when the supply dips. To do that it must see the same voltage as R, so it goes directly across R.

Step 2: **Where to draw it**
Add two parallel plates across the bottom of Fig. 10.1, one lead to the left end of R and one lead to the right end of R. That puts the capacitor in parallel with R.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
State the effect, if any, on the magnitude of the ripple on $V$ when, separately:

1. a capacitor of larger capacitance is used

2. the resistor $R$ has a smaller resistance.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what larger capacitance means for charge stored at the peak and how far the voltage falls before the next peak recharges it.
Hint 2: Think about what smaller load resistance means for the discharge current from the capacitor between peaks.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Larger capacitance means less droop**
A bigger $C$ stores more charge $Q = CV$ at the peak for the same voltage. Between peaks it supplies R, but loses a smaller fraction of its charge, so $V$ falls more slowly and the dip to the next recharge is shallower. Ripple magnitude decreases.

Step 2: **Smaller R means faster discharge**
A smaller $R$ draws a larger current $I = V/R$ from the capacitor. The capacitor discharges faster, so the voltage falls further before the next peak tops it up. Ripple magnitude increases.
